note.question: Will adding rivals reduce a dominant platform's power, or can interoperability and a stronger challenger be more effective than fragmented entry?
note.overview: Competing platforms simultaneously select vectors of net membership fees, users choose at most one platform per side, and network interactions enter platform profits after joining. The paper explicitly defines and studies pure-strategy Nash equilibria, including their existence, uniqueness, dominance, merger, and interoperability comparative statics.

components.label: Model sequence and system structure
components.explanation: Platforms simultaneously announce a vector of net membership fees across market sides. Users observe all fees and choose at most one platform or the outside option on their side. Joining demand is determined by standalone tastes and net fees. After joining, platform-specific interaction benefits arise; the net-fee conduct assumption lets each platform extract those benefits through subsequent interaction charges, so realized demand and network values determine platform profit.

components.label: Pure-strategy Nash equilibrium in platform net fees
components.explanation: The model's equilibrium concept is Pure-strategy Nash equilibrium in platform net fees. Section 2 explicitly defines a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium as a fee profile t in which every platform's vector t^j maximizes its profit against t^{-j}. Proposition 1 supplies the equilibrium first-order pricing identity; Propositions 2-3 give sufficient existence and uniqueness conditions, and later propositions compare selected equilibria across market structure and interoperability policies.
